sources.quote: At least 230 vessels from Europe and the U.S. now support the shadow fleet, which moves an estimated 70 percent of Russia's oil exports.
sources.searcher_note: Pattern: aging Western-owned tankers sold into the shadow fleet, then renamed and reflagged. Ships leaving mainstream trade (U.S. and European owners) for sanctioned trades, with name changes. It does not use U.S.-waters AIS and does not name the lead's ships.

sources.quote: Currently, 927 tankers, approximately 11.6% of the total tanker fleet, are identified as sanctioned.
sources.searcher_note: A world base rate the lead lacks: about 11.6% of all tankers sanctioned, and 'nearly 93% of sanctioned units are over 16 years old'. The lead's U.S.-feed rates (4.6% of older hulls, 3 of 732 newer) sit well below this, which fits the lead's caveat that the U.S. rate may be under the world rate.

sources.quote: a network of aging tankers transporting illicit oil between Iran, Russia, China, and Venezuela
sources.searcher_note: Pattern: an explainer on U.S. seizures of shadow fleet tankers (Skipper ex-Adisa, Bella 1 now Marinera, Olina ex-Minerva M). Renamed, aging, sanctioned tankers, some caught in waters near the U.S. No January 2024 U.S.-waters cohort.

notes: The lead names no individual ships, only counts, so no source can name the entity. No source found tracks the tankers seen in U.S. waters or at U.S. berths in a 2024 window and checks them later against sanctions lists. Coverage found is pattern only: aging Western-owned tankers sold into the shadow fleet and renamed (OCCRP/FTM), world sanctioned-tanker share and age (Breakwave), and U.S. seizures of renamed sanctioned tankers near Venezuela (Atlantic Council, CNN, Lloyd's List on Bella 1 / Marinera, which OFAC sanctioned in June 2024). Nothing in July to September 2026 touched the U.S.-waters angle. 9 searches.
